overview.text: An airplane is an engine-driven, heavier-than-air aircraft supported by air acting on fixed wings, distinguishing it from rotorcraft such as helicopters. As the airplane moves relative to the air, its wings redirect airflow to generate lift; an engine-powered propeller or jet provides thrust to counter drag. Movable controls let a pilot change the aircraft’s climb, descent, and turn. The Wright brothers’ Flyer was a milestone in aviation: after years of glider experiments, Wilbur and Orville Wright made successful powered, controlled flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903. Orville piloted the first; Wilbur’s final flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet.

key_facts.text: The FAA defines an airplane as engine-driven, heavier than air, and supported in flight by air acting on fixed wings.
Lift is produced as a wing moves relative to air and turns the airflow; both upper and lower wing surfaces contribute.
Lift opposes weight, while thrust moves an airplane forward against drag. Small airplanes may use propellers, while larger ones may use jet engines.
The Wright Flyer used a gasoline engine to drive two pusher propellers; its pilot used controls to manage climb, descent, and turns.
On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright piloted the Flyer’s first successful flight at Kitty Hawk; Wilbur’s final flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet.
